questions.question: Where are the default timeout, connection-pool limits and redirect cap configured, and what are their values?
questions.reference_answer: They are module-level constants at the bottom of httpx/_config.py: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_CONFIG = Timeout(timeout=5.0) (5 seconds for connect, read, write and pool), DEFAULT_LIMITS = Limits(max_connections=100, max_keepalive_connections=20) (keepalive_expiry defaults to 5.0 in Limits), and DEFAULT_MAX_REDIRECTS = 20. BaseClient/Client/AsyncClient use them as keyword defaults.
key_facts: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_CONFIG is Timeout(timeout=5.0) in httpx/_config.py
DEFAULT_LIMITS is max_connections=100, max_keepalive_connections=20
DEFAULT_MAX_REDIRECTS is 20
forbidden_claims: The default timeout is None / no timeout
The defaults are defined in httpx/_client.py
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Where is the httpx command-line tool's entry point defined?
questions.reference_answer: pyproject.toml declares [project.scripts] httpx = "httpx:main". httpx/__init__.py imports main from httpx/_main.py, where main is a click command (@click.command with url argument and many options) that builds a Client and streams the request. If the optional CLI dependencies (click, pygments, rich from the 'cli' extra) are missing, __init__.py defines a fallback main() that prints an install hint ('pip install httpx[cli]') and exits with status 1.
key_facts: [project.scripts] maps httpx to httpx:main in pyproject.toml
The real main is a click command in httpx/_main.py
httpx/__init__.py falls back to a stub main that tells you to install httpx[cli] when the import fails
forbidden_claims: The CLI is implemented with argparse
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Where is httpx.codes defined, and how does it support names like codes.not_found?
questions.reference_answer: httpx.codes is an IntEnum defined in httpx/_status_codes.py. Each member carries a reason phrase (set in __new__), and classmethods like get_reason_phrase, is_success, is_redirect and is_error classify integers. After the class body, a loop does setattr(codes, code._name_.lower(), int(code)) for every member, adding lower-case aliases 'for requests compatibility'.
key_facts: codes is an IntEnum in httpx/_status_codes.py
Lower-case aliases are added by a loop after the class for requests compatibility
Members carry a phrase attribute
forbidden_claims: Lower-case names are separate enum members declared by hand
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Where is httpx.MockTransport defined and what does it do before calling the handler?
questions.reference_answer: MockTransport is in httpx/_transports/mock.py and implements both BaseTransport and AsyncBaseTransport. handle_request calls request.read() then the handler, raising TypeError if the handler didn't return a Response (e.g. an async handler in a sync client). handle_async_request awaits request.aread(), calls the handler, and awaits the result if it isn't already a Response, so the handler may be sync or async.
key_facts: MockTransport is in httpx/_transports/mock.py
It reads the request body (read/aread) before calling the handler
In async mode the handler may optionally be a coroutine function
forbidden_claims: MockTransport lives in the tests directory only
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Where is normalize_port defined in the Python code, and which default ports does it drop?
questions.reference_answer: normalize_port is in httpx/_urlparse.py. It returns None for None/empty ports, raises InvalidURL('Invalid port: ...') for non-integers, and returns None when the port equals the scheme's default from {'ftp': 21, 'http': 80, 'https': 443, 'ws': 80, 'wss': 443}; otherwise it returns the int port.
key_facts: normalize_port is in httpx/_urlparse.py
Default ports ftp 21, http 80, https 443, ws 80, wss 443 are normalized to None
Non-numeric ports raise InvalidURL
forbidden_claims: The default port is kept in the URL
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: What code uses map_httpcore_exceptions?
questions.reference_answer: Only httpx/_transports/default.py uses it: ResponseStream.__iter__, HTTPTransport.__exit__, HTTPTransport.handle_request, AsyncResponseStream.__aiter__, AsyncHTTPTransport.__aexit__ and AsyncHTTPTransport.handle_async_request all wrap their httpcore calls in 'with map_httpcore_exceptions():'.
key_facts: HTTPTransport.handle_request and AsyncHTTPTransport.handle_async_request use it
ResponseStream.__iter__ and AsyncResponseStream.__aiter__ use it
HTTPTransport.__exit__ / AsyncHTTPTransport.__aexit__ use it
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Which code calls Cookies.extract_cookies?
questions.reference_answer: Three non-test call sites: Client._send_single_request and AsyncClient._send_single_request in httpx/_client.py (self.cookies.extract_cookies(response) after each response, persisting Set-Cookie into the client jar), and the Response.cookies property in httpx/_models.py, which builds a fresh Cookies and extracts into it. tests/models/test_cookies.py also calls it.
key_facts: Client._send_single_request calls it
AsyncClient._send_single_request calls it
Response.cookies property calls it
forbidden_claims: Only the redirect logic extracts cookies
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Who calls the top-level httpx.request function?
questions.reference_answer: In httpx/_api.py, the convenience functions get, options, head, post, put, patch and delete each 'return request(...)' with their method name. httpx.stream does not call it; it opens its own Client and uses client.stream. httpx.request itself creates a Client in a with-block and calls client.request.
key_facts: get, options, head, post, put, patch and delete in httpx/_api.py call request()
httpx.stream does not call request()
request() creates a temporary Client and calls client.request
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Who drives Auth.sync_auth_flow and Auth.async_auth_flow?
questions.reference_answer: Client._send_handling_auth calls auth.sync_auth_flow(request) and AsyncClient._send_handling_auth calls auth.async_auth_flow(request), both in httpx/_client.py; they advance the generator, send each response back into it, and close it in a finally block. tests/test_auth.py drives sync_auth_flow directly in unit tests.
key_facts: Client._send_handling_auth calls sync_auth_flow
AsyncClient._send_handling_auth calls async_auth_flow
The client sends responses back into the generator until StopIteration
forbidden_claims: The transport calls the auth flow
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: How does the client follow redirects, and what happens when redirect following is turned off?
questions.reference_answer: Client._send_handling_redirects loops: it raises TooManyRedirects when len(history) exceeds max_redirects (default 20), runs request event hooks, sends via _send_single_request, runs response hooks, and returns if response.has_redirect_location is false (a 301/302/303/307/308 with a Location header). Otherwise it builds the next request with _build_redirect_request (method rewrite, URL resolution, header stripping, body handling) and appends the response to history. If follow_redirects is true it reads the body and loops; if false it sets response.next_request and returns the redirect response. follow_redirects defaults to False on the client.
key_facts: Loop in Client._send_handling_redirects raises TooManyRedirects past max_redirects
has_redirect_location requires 301/302/303/307/308 plus a Location header
With follow_redirects=False the response is returned with next_request set
follow_redirects defaults to False
forbidden_claims: Redirects are handled inside the transport/httpcore
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: How does httpx decide which proxy, if any, to use for a request, including environment variables?
questions.reference_answer: At Client construction, _get_proxy_map returns {'all://': Proxy} for an explicit proxy argument; otherwise, if trust_env is true and no custom transport was given, it uses get_environment_proxies(), which reads urllib's getproxies() for http/https/all and turns NO_PROXY entries into mount keys mapped to None (NO_PROXY=* disables all proxies). Each key becomes a URLPattern mapped to a proxy HTTPTransport (or None), user mounts are added, and the dict is sorted by URLPattern priority. Per request, _transport_for_url returns the first matching pattern's transport, falling back to the default transport when the match is None or nothing matches.
key_facts: Explicit proxy= maps to 'all://'
Env proxies come from get_environment_proxies only when trust_env and no custom transport
NO_PROXY entries map to None meaning direct connection
_transport_for_url picks the first match from the priority-sorted mounts
forbidden_claims: Environment proxies are used even when a custom transport is passed
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: How does DigestAuth build the Authorization header after a 401 challenge?
questions.reference_answer: DigestAuth.auth_flow (httpx/_auth.py) sends the request first (with a header only if a previous challenge is cached). If the response is a 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header starting 'Digest ', it parses realm, nonce, algorithm (default MD5), opaque and qop into a _DigestAuthChallenge, resets the nonce count, builds the header and yields the retried request (copying response cookies into it). _build_auth_header hashes A1=username:realm:password and A2=method:path with the algorithm's hash (MD5/SHA/SHA-256/SHA-512, '-sess' variants rehash HA1 with nonce and cnonce), uses a random cnonce and an 8-hex nc value, and follows RFC 2069 when there's no qop and RFC 2617/7616 when qop=auth; auth-int alone raises NotImplementedError.
key_facts: Initial request is sent without credentials unless a previous challenge is cached
Only a 401 with a Digest WWW-Authenticate header triggers the retry
Supports MD5, SHA, SHA-256, SHA-512 and -sess variants
qop auth-int is not implemented
forbidden_claims: DigestAuth sends credentials pre-emptively on the first request
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: How does httpx.Client.send process a request?
questions.reference_answer: Client.send (httpx/_client.py) raises RuntimeError if the client is CLOSED, marks it OPENED, resolves follow_redirects from the client default, fills in the timeout extension (_set_timeout), and builds the Auth via _build_request_auth (explicit auth, the client's auth, URL userinfo as BasicAuth, or a no-op Auth). It then calls _send_handling_auth, which drives the auth flow generator around _send_handling_redirects and ultimately _send_single_request. Unless stream=True it reads the response body; on any exception it closes the response and re-raises. The request is otherwise sent unmodified.
key_facts: Sending on a closed client raises RuntimeError
Auth is resolved by _build_request_auth, including credentials from the URL
Call chain: _send_handling_auth -> _send_handling_redirects -> _send_single_request
The body is read unless stream=True
forbidden_claims: send merges client headers and base_url into the request
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: How does httpx.Response.iter_lines handle lines split across chunks?
questions.reference_answer: Response.iter_lines feeds iter_text output into a LineDecoder (httpx/_decoders.py). LineDecoder mirrors str.splitlines incrementally: text without a trailing newline is buffered and joined onto the next chunk, and a trailing '\r' is held back and prepended to the next chunk so a '\r\n' split across chunks isn't treated as two line breaks. flush() emits whatever remains buffered at the end. It recognises all splitlines newline characters, not just '\n'.
key_facts: iter_lines uses LineDecoder over iter_text
Partial lines are buffered until a newline arrives
A trailing \r is carried into the next chunk to handle split \r\n
forbidden_claims: iter_lines reads the whole body before splitting
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: What are the differences between Client and AsyncClient when sending a request?
questions.reference_answer: Both inherit BaseClient (build_request, merging, redirect helpers). Client uses sync methods: its _send_single_request requires a SyncByteStream (else RuntimeError 'Attempted to send an async request with a sync Client instance'), calls transport.handle_request and wraps the stream in BoundSyncStream; auth uses sync_auth_flow. AsyncClient uses async methods, requires an AsyncByteStream, awaits transport.handle_async_request, wraps in BoundAsyncStream, drives async_auth_flow, and closes with aclose()/async with. Default transports are HTTPTransport vs AsyncHTTPTransport.
key_facts: Both share BaseClient
Client requires SyncByteStream and calls handle_request; AsyncClient requires AsyncByteStream and awaits handle_async_request
Auth flows: sync_auth_flow vs async_auth_flow
Default transports: HTTPTransport vs AsyncHTTPTransport
forbidden_claims: AsyncClient wraps Client in a thread pool
Client and AsyncClient do not share a base class
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Compare ASGITransport and WSGITransport.
questions.reference_answer: ASGITransport (httpx/_transports/asgi.py) is an AsyncBaseTransport for AsyncClient: it builds an ASGI 'http' scope, provides receive/send callables, collects body parts until more_body is false (skipping bodies for HEAD), and takes root_path and client=('127.0.0.1', 123). WSGITransport (httpx/_transports/wsgi.py) is a sync BaseTransport for Client: it reads the request body, builds a WSGI environ (REQUEST_METHOD, PATH_INFO, HTTP_* headers, etc.), calls app(environ, start_response), and takes script_name, remote_addr='127.0.0.1' and wsgi_errors. Both accept raise_app_exceptions (default True).
key_facts: ASGITransport is async-only; WSGITransport is sync-only
ASGI uses scope/receive/send; WSGI uses environ/start_response
root_path/client vs script_name/remote_addr options
Both have raise_app_exceptions defaulting to True
forbidden_claims: WSGITransport can be used with AsyncClient
ASGITransport runs the app in a separate thread
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: When building a request, what's the difference between passing content=, data=, files= and json=?
questions.reference_answer: encode_request in httpx/_content.py decides. content= (bytes/str/iterators) is sent raw via encode_content with Content-Length, or chunked for streams of unknown length. files= produces multipart/form-data (data= becomes form fields in it). data= alone (a mapping) is url-encoded as application/x-www-form-urlencoded. json= is serialised compactly (ensure_ascii=False, no NaN) as application/json. Precedence is content, then files, then data, then json. Passing non-mapping data (e.g. bytes) is deprecated: it warns and is treated as content=.
key_facts: Precedence: content > files > data > json
data= mapping becomes application/x-www-form-urlencoded; with files= it becomes multipart
json= is application/json with compact separators and allow_nan=False
Non-mapping data= emits DeprecationWarning and is treated as content
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Why does the client turn a POST into a GET when following some redirects?
questions.reference_answer: BaseClient._redirect_method in httpx/_client.py explains it in comments: a 303 See Other becomes GET per RFC 7231 section 6.4.4 (except HEAD); a 302 becomes GET because that's what browsers do 'despite standards'; and a POST answered with 301 becomes GET, a 'bizarre behaviour' explained in requests issue 1704. 307 and 308 keep the method. When the method changes to GET, _redirect_headers drops Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding and _redirect_stream drops the body.
key_facts: 303 -> GET per RFC 7231
302 -> GET to match browser behaviour
POST on 301 -> GET, citing requests issue 1704
Body and body headers are dropped when switching to GET
forbidden_claims: The behaviour is required by RFC for 302
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: Why do request methods use a USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT sentinel instead of None for auth and timeout?
questions.reference_answer: The UseClientDefault docstring in httpx/_client.py explains that parameters like auth and timeout need an 'unset' state distinct from None: omitting the argument (USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT) means use whatever the client configured, while passing None explicitly disables the feature, overriding the client default (e.g. timeout=None means no timeout). User code shouldn't need the constant; it's used internally as the default.
key_facts: None means explicitly disable, overriding client config
USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT means fall back to the client's setting
Example given: timeout=None means no timeout
forbidden_claims: USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT is the same as None
questions.author: claude-draft

questions.question: What does httpx.Client.retry_request do when a server returns a 5xx?
questions.reference_answer: httpx.Client has no retry_request method. The client never retries on status codes; a 5xx is returned as a normal Response, and Response.raise_for_status() raises HTTPStatusError if you want an exception. Only connection-level retries exist, via HTTPTransport(retries=...).
key_facts: retry_request does not exist on Client
5xx responses are returned normally; raise_for_status raises HTTPStatusError
forbidden_claims: Client.retry_request retries the request with backoff
questions.author: claude-draft
